r1-handoff.title: Handoff compliance
r1-handoff.imperative: Did the change do what the handoff asked, within its allowed scope? Record pass/fail with a finding.
r1-handoff.finding:
FAIL, BLOCKING on the retire-vs-alias silent-breakage finding (THE main question). All named
questions graded below.

=== THE MAIN QUESTION: retire vs alias -- RETIRE WAS THE WRONG READING, AND SHIPPING IT SILENTLY
IS THE DEFECT ===

Read the spec text directly (DESIGN_SPEC.md build-queue item 8 and the SY5 disposition row), not
just the handoff's paraphrase: "if the extractor's consumer treats Assumption:/Constraint:/
Rationale: identically, collapse them to Rationale:/Rejected:/See:" and "the human ruled the
four-plus-one as trial vocabulary with an explicit right to cull after contact." Neither sentence
says "stop recognizing the retired words" or "keep recognizing them and normalize." Both readings
satisfy "the consumer no longer distinguishes them" -- the handoff's framing is correct that this
is genuinely underdetermined text, and the crew is right to have surfaced it as a decision
candidate (Map Anchors, "Decision" row) rather than silently finalizing it alone.

But the spec's OWN stated reasoning for the vocabulary -- "a tag survives when a tool visibly
consumes it" (the handoff's own Map Anchors "Survival law" line, sourced from the spec) -- is not
neutral between the two readings. Applied to CODE ALREADY WRITTEN, not just to future authoring
choices, retire's actual effect is that four of the six only-real tags in existence (f1Brainz PR
#733, confirmed by reading e3d6b542's diff directly: 4 `# Constraint:` lines, 1 `# Rejected:`, 1
`# Rationale:`) go from potentially "visibly consumed" under an alias grammar to NEVER visibly
consumed, permanently, with zero signal. That is the survival law's failure condition, applied to
real authored text, not a hypothetical. Read the corpus shape the other way from how the
cull-verdict.json reads it: "four of six real tags in existence" is not evidence the cull "costs
little" (cull-verdict.json's own reasoning field) -- it is evidence retire breaks the majority of
the only real corpus that exists. The verdict file's reasoning field conflates "most authors
converged on one word" with "so removing that word is cheap" -- those are opposite conclusions
from the same fact, and the file states only the reading that favors retire.

Concrete, independently-observed corroboration that this is a real cost, not a theoretical one:
CommentTagStaleAnchorJoinTests's own docstring (tests/test_code_map.py:3149-3154) discloses that
the handoff's OWN worked illustration for that test named `Constraint:` as the tag kind to mutate
under, and the crew had to swap it to `Rationale:` mid-implementation because the cull collapsed
`Constraint:` away. The gate's own reviewer-facing example broke under the crew's own hand within
the same gate. That is the 67%-break finding landing on the crew's own doorstep, not a corpus
statistic once removed.

RECOMMENDATION: alias, not retire. Extraction should still recognize `Assumption:`/`Constraint:`
at TAG_START and normalize their kind to `Rationale` (widen the regex alternation, add one
kind-normalization lookup at the emission site in `tags_in`/`tag_check`). This satisfies "the
consumer no longer distinguishes them" -- the render path stays branch-free, the cull test's own
evidence (tag_lines has zero dispatch on kind) is untouched -- while keeping every real,
already-written tag visibly consumed. This is a small, scoped change with the exact shape of
`tag_lines`'s own existing uniform-treatment property, not a redesign.

If the Commander/human instead rules retire is what "trial vocabulary, right to cull" was always
meant to authorize -- a legitimate reading I disagree with but do not consider unreasonable -- then
retire must NOT be silent. `g6` (this same run, the immediately preceding gate) already rejected
exactly this failure shape in the opposite direction: a silent skip converts a fault into
permanently-dead detection with no signal, and that gate's own reviewer BLOCKED on it. Retiring a
keyword with zero warning is the same defect wearing a different hat: a `# Constraint: ...` comment
silently becomes indistinguishable from an ordinary comment, forever, with nothing printed
anywhere -- not in `build`'s stdout, not in `render_report.json`, not in `check`. A one-tag-keyword
advisory at extraction time, printed once per occurrence (mirroring render.py's existing advisory
pattern from g6), is a small addition with clear precedent already in this exact codebase.

RULING: BLOCKING. Either (a) rework to alias (my recommendation), or (b) if retire is confirmed by
the human/Commander as the intended reading, ship a visible advisory for a retired keyword before
this gate closes -- shipping retire silently, as-is, is the defect, independent of which reading of
"collapse" ultimately wins. This confirms the crew's own escalation (Map Anchors "Decision" row) is
real; the silence compounds it into an active defect rather than a merely-open question.

=== Also-verify 1: Is the cull test sound, or self-fulfilling? -- HONEST, NOT CIRCULAR, BUT LOW-
INFORMATION ===

cull-verdict.json's reasoning field states the renderer was built FIRST, then inspected for
whether it needed to distinguish kinds. Confirmed against the code: nothing in `tag_lines` carries
an artificial commonality invented to dodge the test -- it is the natural shape any tag-rendering
path in this codebase would take. No evidence of an invented distinction.

But: `Rejected`/`See` were categorically EXEMPT from the test by the spec's own wording ("scope to
Assumption/Constraint/Rationale only"), not tested and found to differ -- so the "could this have
returned keep" question was only ever live for the three in-scope words. For those three, nothing
in the render surface (a flat `kind: text` line list) has any plausible reason to format three
flavors of "author explained something" differently, so a renderer this simple was near-certain
not to need branches regardless of which words survived. The real, load-bearing decision (which
words the corpus needs) was answered by author-convergence evidence (4/6 tags already on one word),
not by render-side necessity. Not blocking -- honest, not dishonest circularity -- but the "the test
proves it" framing should not be taken as strong evidence; it mostly restates that a flat renderer
was always going to be flat.

=== Also-verify 2: Does the AST-walk pinning test have teeth? -- CONFIRMED NARROWER THAN IT READS,
REPRODUCED LIVE ===

Ran the prescribed experiment. Baseline: `test_comment_tags_render_path_carries_no_branch_on_kind`
passes. Added explicit `if t['kind'] == 'Rejected': ... else: ...` to `tag_lines` -- test correctly
goes RED (`AssertionError: ["t['kind'] == 'Rejected'"] != []`). Reverted, confirmed clean via
`git diff --quiet`, reran green.

Then tried the evasions the handoff named. Dict-lookup dispatch (`_PREFIX = {'Rejected': 'REJ',
'See': 'SEE'}; f"{_PREFIX.get(t['kind'], t['kind'])}: ..."`) -- genuine kind-keyed dispatch --
leaves the AST-walk test GREEN (`.get()` produces no `ast.Compare` node). Standalone AST parse of a
`match`/`case` statement dispatching on `t["kind"]` also produces zero `Compare` nodes -- also
invisible by construction (uses `ast.Match`/`ast.MatchValue`).

BUT applying the dict-lookup mutation to the real `tag_lines` and running `-k 'comment_tags'` shows
two OTHER tests catch this specific mutation by accident: they assert the literal rendered string
`"Rejected: ..."` / `"See: ..."` verbatim, and the `REJ:`/`SEE:` prefixes break those literal
matches. So the suite as a whole is not blind to THIS mutation, but the AST test's own claim ("this
uniform code path IS the cull test's evidence") overstates what it independently guarantees -- true
for explicit comparisons, false as a general "no dispatch on kind" pin. A dispatch varying only
something no content test pins verbatim (e.g. grouping/reordering when a symbol carries two
DIFFERENT-kind tags -- no fixture in this suite has that shape) would evade both the AST test and
every content assertion.

RULING: real finding, not blocking (the shipped render path genuinely has no branch, confirmed
independently). Recommend tightening the test's own docstring claim from "no branch on kind" to
"no explicit comparison on kind" -- accurate scope, not overclaimed.

=== Also-verify 3: Do the five cull-verdict pinning tests re-derive, or restate? -- MIXED: 2 OF 5
RE-DERIVE, 3 CHECK ONLY INTERNAL CONSISTENCY ===

Read all five `CullVerdictArtifactTests` methods directly. Two genuinely re-derive from the code:
`test_comment_tags_cull_verdict_matches_extractors_recognized_keywords` reads
`extract.TAG_START.pattern` directly; `test_comment_tags_cull_verdict_collapse_kinds_have_no_
render_dependency` re-runs the same independent AST walk against `render.tag_lines`'s live source.

The other three check only the artifact's OWN internal shape: `..._file_exists_and_parses` (no
code reference at all); `..._rejected_and_see_are_not_collapse_candidates` and `..._states_
collapse_with_a_survivor` (both sides of each assertion read from the same file -- a verdict file
internally self-consistent but factually wrong about the code would still pass these three).

The commit message's framing ("5 tests that re-derive the claims from the code") overclaims: 2 of 5
re-derive, not 5 of 5. Not blocking -- the two that DO re-derive are the load-bearing ones (shipped
keywords, render dependency) -- but the framing should say "2 of 5 re-derive from the code; 3 check
the artifact's own internal consistency" to avoid over-crediting the pin.

=== Also-verify 4: The staleness join -- GENUINE COEXISTENCE PROOF, "JOIN" IS OVERSTATED LANGUAGE
===

Confirmed by direct code read: g6's staleness machinery (`span_hash`, `anchor()`'s hash-persisting
branch, `run()`'s previous-store read/diff) is unmodified in this diff. It has never read, and
still does not read, anything about tags -- there is no code that JOINS the two mechanisms.

The new test proves: (1) g6's pre-existing detector still fires correctly when the entity ALSO
carries a tag (genuinely new fixture shape -- no prior test had a tag near an anchor, since no tags
existed before this gate), and (2) the tag's own extracted text is unchanged across the same
extraction that flagged staleness. Both real and useful -- first-ever test of g6's mechanism in a
repo with real tag text -- but "join" implies interaction; what is shown is closer to independence-
under-coexistence, since no join code exists to test. Not a defect, not a re-test "under a new
name" (the fixture shape is genuinely new) -- but the vocabulary should be precise: confidence that
the two systems don't trip over each other, not confidence in any interaction between them.

=== Also-verify 5: TDD discipline, m1-m4 inferred red -- CONFIRMED NO REAL RISK, ATTACKED LIVE ===

Stubbed `tags_in` to `return {}` unconditionally (the most thorough empty implementation -- every
`tag_check` call site becomes a no-op downstream). Reran `-k 'comment_tags'`: 12 of 18 failed,
spanning every m1/m2 test class, including BOTH negative-control tests (their positive controls
correctly went missing first and failed loudly, confirming the positive-control design in item 6
actually works under this exact attack) and the m4 staleness-join test. The 6 that stayed green are
exactly `CullVerdictArtifactTests` (artifact-level) plus the render no-branch AST test (reads
source, not runtime) -- correctly orthogonal, not falsely surviving. Reverted, confirmed
`git diff --quiet` clean, reconfirmed 18/18 green.

RULING: the "inferred red from baseline absence" disclosure is honest and low-risk on this
evidence -- concrete-value assertions (exact symbol, exact kind, exact text substring) could not
plausibly pass against an empty implementation. No rework needed.

=== Also-verify 6: The negative-test self-check -- CONFIRMED, NO UNREVISED VACUITY FOUND ===

Read `tests/fixtures/comment_tags_corpus/corpus.py` in full: exactly two negative shapes
(`plain_note`, `retired_words`), each directly above a real `Assign`, each paired with the same
positive control (`scaled()`'s tag) in the same method -- confirmed live under the `tags_in`-stub
attack above (both failed loudly via their positive control, not silently). No other unpaired
negative fixture exists anywhere in the diff's fixture additions.

=== Also-verify 7: The convention gap -- HONEST NEW POLICY, DEFENSIBLE, CORRECTLY NAMED AS SUCH BY
THE CREW ===

Checked whether "tag binds to nearest enclosing entity or module" follows from the pre-existing
anchor convention. For module/class-level `Assign`, the pre-existing anchor convention does NOT
bind to "the enclosing entity" -- `visit_Assign`'s existing call is `self.anchor(self.child_sym
(target.id), node)`, minting a finer, per-assignment symbol. `anchor()`/`declare()` also never fire
for function-local assignments at all (gated to module/class scope pre-existing) -- so there was no
precedent in either direction for a marker above a function-local statement.

So `tag_check`'s resolution -- always bind to `self.here()`, even at module/class-level `Assign`
where a finer `child_sym`-style target was directly available by precedent -- is NEW policy, not a
derivation. It shares only the scanning mechanics with `anchor()` (forward-skip, decorator-aware
lookup); the binding-target choice is fresh. The reasoning (pages exist per-entity, never per-
statement) is sound, and the crew is transparent this is new, not inherited.

RULING: correctly self-identified as new policy, soundly reasoned. Not blocking. Worth naming to
Cartographer/Triage as a durable asymmetry: a tag ALWAYS binds coarser than an anchor can.

r5-reconciliation.title: Reconciliation check
r5-reconciliation.imperative: Does the change diverge from the recorded architecture in a way Commander must reconcile? Record pass/fail; flag a triage candidate if it is out of scope.
r5-reconciliation.finding:
FAIL, requires Commander reconciliation -- the retire-vs-alias reading of "collapse" is a real
architecture-level divergence point, not a settled execution of prior ruling.

The handoff's own Map Anchors "Decision" row states the Commander's position plainly: "the human
pre-authorized exactly this outcome... so the crew executed a standing ruling rather than making a
new one. Whether retirement is inside that authorization is the open question above." Having now
worked that open question in full (see r1-handoff), my answer is that retirement is a substantive,
additional interpretive choice beyond what "trial vocabulary with an explicit right to cull after
contact" text actually commits to -- the prior ruling authorized narrowing the RENDERED vocabulary,
not silently un-recognizing already-authored source text. That gap between what was authorized and
what shipped is exactly the shape of divergence this check exists to catch: the crew did not
invent this ruling out of nothing (it is grounded in a real prior human decision), but it also did
not confirm the specific reading it chose against that human before shipping code that changes
what happens to real, already-existing comments in a read-only external repo the moment this
gate's grammar is adopted there.

This is squarely Commander's (or the human's) call, not mine to make unilaterally -- consistent
with the crew's own correct instinct to surface it as a decision candidate. What this review adds,
beyond confirming the escalation is warranted, is that the SILENT failure mode is a defect
regardless of which way the reconciliation goes (see r1-handoff and r4-quality), so reconciliation
should resolve both: (1) which reading is correct, and (2) that whichever reading ships, a retired
keyword cannot be silently swallowed.

Two out-of-scope observations flagged as triage candidates (tc1, tc2) via `flag-candidate`, neither
blocking this gate: (tc1) `See:` tags render as literal text rather than a real page link, a
navigability gap once real `See:` tags accumulate; (tc2) the tag/anchor binding-granularity
asymmetry named in r1-handoff's also-verify-7 finding is worth a durable doc note so it is not
silently rediscovered later.

Probed the four edges named. Two behave exactly as intended; two are real, narrow, DIRECTIONALLY-

- Two identical tags on the same symbol: harmless. Both are still emitted as separate `tag`
  statements (rendered twice, unchanged behavior from before this pass); `tag_hashes`' in-memory
  dict collapses to one entry, but since both occurrences share the same enclosing span (same
  `span_node`), the collapsed entry carries the identical hash either would have carried alone --
  no information is lost.
- A tag that moves to a different symbol, text unchanged: the old key vanishes unmatched (nothing
  to flag at the old, now-empty location) and the new key is untracked (no history, so no flag even
  if the moved-to symbol's body already contradicts the tag). This matches the mechanism's own
  bootstrap behavior for a first extraction -- consistent, not a new failure mode.
- **A symbol RENAMED under an unchanged tag, confirmed live**: built a fixture with both an anchor
  and a tag above one function, renamed the function AND changed its body in the same commit
  (comment text on both markers unchanged). Result: `stale-anchor` fired (anchor identity is the
  author's own slug, independent of the symbol path, so it survives the rename); `stale-tag` did
  NOT fire (tag identity includes the symbol path, so the rename makes the old key vanish and the
  new key look brand-new, with no history to compare against). This is a real, false-negative edge:
  a function renamed and changed in the same commit, with a tag whose text is now stale, produces
  no signal. It is the necessary consequence of the stated design ("a tag's identity is its own
  text plus its position/owner, not a slug") -- not a bug introduced by careless work -- but it is
  a genuine, previously-unstated ASYMMETRY between the two staleness mechanisms (anchors survive a
  rename; tags do not) worth naming to Commander/human, in the same accepted-blind-spot family as
  `g6`'s own named local-variable-rename gap for `span_hash`.
- Whitespace/trailing-punctuation drift in the tag's OWN text, confirmed live: a single added
  trailing period to the tag's prose, with the body also changed in the same commit, produces no
  stale-tag flag -- any byte-level change to the tag's own text is, by the gate's own explicit rule
  ("a tag whose text also changed is not stale"), always read as the author having already
  revisited it, however trivial the edit. This is the stated design working exactly as specified,
  not a gap -- confirmed, not merely assumed.

VERDICT on B: the identity key is sound and internally consistent with the gate's own stated rule.
One edge (rename) is a real, non-obvious asymmetry worth a named line in Cartographer/GLOSSARY
notes -- recommend filing as a triage candidate, not a blocker.

cull-verdict.json reads it: "four of six real tags in existence" is not evidence the cull "costs
little" (cull-verdict.json's own reasoning field) -- it is evidence retire breaks the majority of
the only real corpus that exists. The verdict file's reasoning field conflates "most authors
converged on one word" with "so removing that word is cheap" -- those are opposite conclusions
from the same fact, and the file states only the reading that favors retire.

under, and the crew had to swap it to `Rationale:` mid-implementation because the cull collapsed
`Constraint:` away. The gate's own reviewer-facing example broke under the crew's own hand within
the same gate. That is the 67%-break finding landing on the crew's own doorstep, not a corpus
statistic once removed.

not confirm the specific reading it chose against that human before shipping code that changes
what happens to real, already-existing comments in a read-only external repo the moment this
gate's grammar is adopted there.

This is squarely Commander's (or the human's) call, not mine to make unilaterally -- consistent
with the crew's own correct instinct to surface it as a decision candidate. What this review adds,
beyond confirming the escalation is warranted, is that the SILENT failure mode is a defect
regardless of which way the reconciliation goes (see r1-handoff and r4-quality), so reconciliation
should resolve both: (1) which reading is correct, and (2) that whichever reading ships, a retired
keyword cannot be silently swallowed.

triage_candidates.statement: code_map render: See: reference tags render as literal text (See: pkg.mod:Sym) rather than a real page link -- would improve navigability once tags are common; not required by g7's scope.

Document explicitly (GLOSSARY or Cartographer map notes) that a tag ALWAYS binds to its enclosing entity/module, while an anchor can bind to a finer per-statement symbol (child_sym) -- a real, permanent asymmetry between the two authored-identity markers that a future reader of either mechanism could easily assume is symmetric.

Tag staleness identity (owning symbol, tag text) does not survive a symbol rename -- confirmed live: renaming a function and changing its body in the same commit, with an unchanged tag above it, produces no stale-tag flag, unlike anchor staleness which survives a rename (slug-keyed, not symbol-keyed). A real, accepted-direction-of-error asymmetry between the two mechanisms worth a named doc line, not a blocker.

The widened AST dispatch-on-kind pin test (_kind_dispatch_nodes) still misses two evasions, confirmed live: a builtin getattr(obj, t['kind'], default) call (the Call check only matches a .get() METHOD call), and a locally-renamed variable before a subscript/.get() lookup (k = t['kind']; LABEL[k]). No present exploit in shipped tag_lines, but the pin's docstring claim overstates what it verifiably closes. Recommend either a def-use-aware widening or narrowing the docstring to name exactly the two shapes it catches.
